085 - Homeland and Philosophy - For Your: Homeland is the Showtime espionage thriller (2011-2020) about Carrie Mathison, a brilliant, bipolar CIA officer convinced that Nicholas Brody, a Marine rescued after years as a prisoner of war, has been turned by al-Qaeda. The show's mind games make it philosophy-ready: essays here ask whether the brainwashed Brody is still the same person, what his PTSD does to his identity, whether suicide can ever be justified, whether terrorists' morality needs God, and how Carrie's colluding roles of agent, patient, and lover can be reconciled.
086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book I: Girls was Lena Dunham's HBO comedy-drama (2012-2017) about four self-absorbed twenty-something women muddling through work, sex, and friendship in Brooklyn, famous for making its heroine Hannah memorably unlikable. That rawness is why it earns a philosophy book: essays debate whether portraying degrading sex can be anti-feminist, why the show resists Adorno's culture industry when Friends did not, whether Adam's run across Brooklyn was truly heroic, and whether narcissists like Hannah and Jessa can live an examined, meaningful life.
087 - Adventure Time and Philosophy - Th: Adventure Time is Cartoon Network's beloved animated series (2010-2018) following Finn the boy and Jake the shapeshifting dog through the surreal post-apocalyptic Land of Ooo, praised for sneaking surprisingly heavy ideas into a kids' cartoon. This book takes the show at its word: essays ask whether Finn's faith in magic over Princess Bubblegum's science stunts his moral growth, what makes Ice King a tragic figure rather than a villain, when Princess Bubblegum's parental rule over candy citizens is legitimate, and whether Simon's crown-borne self-sacrifice was heroic.
088 - Justified and Philosophy - Shoot F: Justified was FX's crime drama (2010-2015) about Raylan Givens, an Old West-style US Marshal policing his own home turf of Harlan County, Kentucky, where coal poverty and crime run deep. Its pilot poses the book's driving question: when Raylan gives a hitman until sundown to leave town and then shoots him, is that justice or murder with a badge? Essays probe proactive policing and the war on drugs, Boyd Crowder's coal-country rebellion through Hegel, the show's racial casting patterns, coolness as a virtue, and whether Raylan ever really knows who done it.
089 - Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Th: Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, made computers, music players, phones, and animated films (through Pixar) central to modern life while being by many accounts petulant and cruel; this book neither canonizes nor demonizes him. Essays examine his famous 'reality distortion field' through the ethics of deception, ask whether a counterculture hippie capitalist is a contradiction, grade him against Plato's cardinal virtues, explore how Pixar films taught a generation to recognize personhood in non-humans, and ask whether American schools could ever produce an entrepreneurial mind like his.
090 - Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to: Dracula is Bram Stoker's 1897 Gothic novel about the Transylvanian vampire who moves to London to feed on the living, the source of over a century of film adaptations and the archetype of the vampire itself. This book asks why we keep inviting the Count into our evenings: essays weigh whether eternal life would be a curse of endless boredom, map Kierkegaard's stages of life onto Harker, Mina, and Van Helsing, read the blood exchange through Plotinus, and ask why a monster who obeys no morality still cannot enter without an invitation.
091 - It's Always Sunny and Philosophy -: It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia is FX's long-running dark sitcom (since 2005) about 'the Gang,' five vain, amoral bar owners whose schemes ruin everyone around them without a flicker of remorse. Their total badness makes them a strange philosophical laboratory: essays use the Gang's values to compare against Homer's heroes, test hedonism through Nozick's experience machine, ask whether Charlie's lucky guesses amount to knowledge in Gettier's sense, diagnose CharDee MacDennis through Freud's id, ego, and superego, and pin down what makes the McPoyle brothers genuinely creepy.
092 - Orange Is the New Black and Philos: Orange Is the New Black is the Netflix ensemble drama (2013-2019), adapted from Piper Kerman's memoir, about a privileged white woman serving time in a federal women's prison and the far more precarious inmates around her. Prison makes it natural philosophy territory: essays apply Sartre's bad faith to guards and lovers, Bentham's panopticon and Foucault to life under surveillance, Nietzsche to Sophia Burset's transition, and critical scrutiny to the show's racial framing, while asking what prisoners owe each other and whether anyone at Litchfield is authentic.
093 - More Doctor Who and Philosophy - R: Doctor Who is the BBC's science-fiction institution (since 1963) about the Doctor, a time-traveling alien who regenerates into a new body and face instead of dying, touring the universe in a police box bigger on the inside. This follow-up volume chases the show's signature puzzles: could Clara really exist as multiple scattered echoes, does the Doctor's drift from self-described coward to gun-toting hero track the War on Terror, is 'Am I a good man?' answerable across regenerations, and how the show's shifting, regenerating format makes it a metaphor for television itself.
094 - Divergent and Philosophy - The Fac: Divergent is Veronica Roth's dystopian YA series (2011-2013) and film franchise set in a ruined Chicago where society is sorted into five virtue-based factions, until Tris Prior's 'Divergence' proves she cannot be filed under any single one. The setup is a working philosophy experiment: essays read the faction serums against medicating 'difficult' children, test Abnegation's selflessness through Buddhist practice and Nietzsche's slave morality, compare the controlling Bureau to the Tuskegee study, and argue, with the editor, that Tris retraces Plato's cave, discovering the faction life is a lie worth dying for.
